history.content: What is the recommended management for Striga hermonthica on sorghum?

history.content: My sorghum plants stay short and yellow even though the rains are good, what is happening?

history.content: How can I control Striga witchweed on my sorghum field?

draws.answer: Striga, also called sorghum striga, is the weed that climbs and consumes the maize roots. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing 3 to 5 grains per pocket at 3 to 5 cm depth. Do not go beyond 3 grains per pocket, which lets the pocket seeds settle and reduces the weed. Weed the sorghum 2 to 3 times while the plants are small and keep the seedlings from 15 to 20 days. After the plants reach panicle initiation, apply 2 to 3 kg of the recommended NPK fertilizer per hectare. Then, plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field to cut the Striga. For a precise variety recommendation and the exact fertilizer dose, go to ICAT.

Striga witchweed is controlled by sowing a striga tolerant sorghum variety together with or in rotation with your sorghum, and by removing the weeds at harvest. First, choose a striga tolerant sorghum variety that matches your local rains. Then plant the sorghum early and follow the recommended close spacing to reduce weed pressure. After harvesting, work to clear or bury all Striga plants before they flower. If you need help selecting a tolerant variety, see ICAT.

history.content: I see a purple flowered weed clinging around the base of my short sorghum plants, what should I do?

draws.answer: You mentioned a purple-flowered weed is growing near your short sorghum plants and you want to know what to do. That weed is a common short sorghum pest and you need to decide which variety to use next season. First, look at the leaves: a uniform pale yellow on older lower leaves shows a nitrogen deficiency, so you should not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide. Second, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or by burying residues instead of burning them. Third, plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Fourth, go to ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot. I cannot give you a specific fertilizer recommendation.

The purple-flowered weed is a sign of groundnut rosette, which causes young leaves to curl upward. First, walk through your field and pull out the severely affected groundnut plants, destroying them. Then, plan to plant a tolerant groundnut variety in the next season to avoid the disease. After that, avoid sowing groundnut on the same land year after year, rotate with cereals rather than planting groundnut together. If you need help with resistant varieties, go to ICAT.

history.content: What is Cassava brown streak virus and how can I manage it?

Then, when you plant again, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and plant those cuttings. history.content: why must we vaccinate healthy animals during outbreak

draws.answer: Vaccinating healthy animals stops the virus from spreading further before it kills them. The vaccine protects the animals but also limits the disease's spread. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can tell which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. It is not Striga, it is a nitrogen shortage because the plants are short of nitrogen. Look at the leaves: yellowing that starts at the bottom and climbs is nitrogen deficiency, not a virus. Because it is a nitrogen shortage, you must open a shallow drainage channel to let water run off the plot, then side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing up on schedule. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: There is no way to make a stronger insecticide mix; the guidelines say the opposite. What the label asks for is a product that has the product name on it and is approved for what you grow and where, and you use it at the rate the label says. Read it. If the label is missing it is a problem to ask ICAT about, not a guess.

You cannot mix the two insecticides; they are not formulated to combine. The approved product in the label is a specific product and a concentration, and mixing two products changes both. The label tells you to wear gloves and cover your mouth and nose, and it tells you not to taste the product, so you can't accidentally mix products meant for different crops or for different pests. history.content: why sorghum stays stunted yellow

Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word because mineral fertilizer alone often fails on depleted soils. First restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or burying residues instead of burning them. After that, plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper dose for your plot.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: There is no way to make a stronger insecticide mix; the guidelines say the opposite. Mixing two or more active ingredients does not give you a higher product, and it creates an unknown product, which is not something to guess. What the label asks for is a product that has the product name on it and is approved for what you grow and where, and you use it at the rate the label says. Read it. If the label is missing it is a problem to ask ICAT about, not a guess.

You cannot mix the two insecticides; they are not formulated to combine. The approved product in the label is a specific product and a concentration, and mixing two products changes both. The label tells you to wear gloves and cover your mouth and nose, and it tells you not to taste the product, so you can't accidentally mix products meant for different crops or for different pests. Use the approved product at the label rate, and if it is not there, ask ICAT for the product's name and its rate. If the pest is not on the label, take a leaf or a fruit to ICAT for confirmation before you choose a new product.

history.content: My goats have a mucky discharge from their eyes and some are dying quickly. What steps must I take?

draws.answer: Your goats are dealing with a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. You need to call the veterinary service the same day because only they can identify the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick goats in the shade, ensure clean water is available and do not make them walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick goat. Do not reuse the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service is the only place to obtain the proper medication.

So ask the supplier of the product you are mixing for the exact rate, and ask ICAT before you mix any product at all.

per_item.reference: The symptoms point to cassava mosaic disease because the leaf deformation is the key tell, while the brown root rot belongs to cassava brown streak disease. history.content: My field shows cassava leaves that are yellow and twisted, but I also notice some brown rot in the roots. Which disease am I dealing with?

draws.answer: It is cassava mosaic disease. First, uproot and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled, twisted or stunted. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy, avoiding mottled or deformed stems. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep a uniform, well-fed stand that is less affected by the disease. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Those symptoms are caused by cassava mosaic disease, not brown rot. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

per_item.reference: Striga hermonthica is the witchweed that appears as a purple/pink flowered weed at the base of stunted sorghum. Pull the weed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted material so the seed does not spread. Apply organic manure together with a small amount of urea to the soil to weaken the parasite and strengthen the crop. Earth up the soil after fertilising. Rotate or intercrop with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For badly infested fields, go to ICAT for tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: What steps should I take to manage Striga hermonthica in my sorghum crop?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed attacking sorghum that causes awns. Plant a legume such as cowpea or groundnut in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nodules stay in the soil. Grow the legume early, before the plants flower, and cut the stems at the soil surface. Do not spray any fungicide because no spray cures an infected plant. For a legume recommendation, see ICAT.

Striga is the parasitic plant that attaches itself to sorghum and pulls nitrogen up. First, stop using a striga tolerant sorghum variety, which reduces the need for the weed. Second, rotate your sorghum with a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to pull the striga plant out of the soil. Third, pull the striga plants out before they flower and destroy them. Fourth, ask ICAT for a striga tolerant variety to plant next season. If you need help with variety selection, ICAT is the service to contact.

per_item.reference: It is not nutrient deficiency, it is Striga, the parasitic weed that attaches to roots and robs the plant. Nutrient deficiency shows no attached weed, while Striga appears as a purple or pink-flowered weed clinging around the base of stunted plants. Because it is Striga, you must pull the weeds by hand before they flower and burn them to stop seed spread. After removal, add organic manure plus some urea, then earth up the soil. Finally, rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to reduce the seed bank. For tolerant varieties and a rotation plan, consult ICAT.

history.content: My sorghum has Striga, it must be nutrient deficiency, so I just add fertilizer

draws.answer: It is not Striga, it is a nitrogen deficiency caused by the legume being grown in the same year. Striga is the same plant that grows on top of a legume, not the soil around it; it is the legume that removes nitrogen from the soil, not a deficiency. To tell them apart you look at the plants: Striga gives a dense, purple-flavored knot where it attaches, and it takes its place on the plant; a deficiency shows a uniform pale yellowing of the older lower leaves while the young top leaves stay greener. Because it is a deficiency, you must not grow a legume this year, rotate with a legume such as cowpea or soybean, and bring back organic matter with manure or compost. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK or a systemic fungicide, which will not turn the plant green. Ask ICAT to analyse your soil and give the right dose.

It is not nutrient deficiency, it is a parasitic problem. Striga is the fungus that attaches itself to the stem, pulling plant matter and leaving no roots. Nutrient deficiency shows as a gradual yellowing that starts on older leaves and worsens each year, while a fungus needs a fungicide. Because it is a parasite, you must pull out and destroy the heavily affected plants. After that, weed the field and keep the whole area free of weeds that can host it between crops. Then plant a cereal to use the nitrogen left by the legumes. If you later notice a fungus on the stem, you need a professional. I cannot give you a specific product or dose for this.

history.content: I see a pink-flowered weed clinging to the base of my sorghum and the plants look short. What should I do?

draws.answer: You are dealing with striga in sorghum, and you need to sow a striga-tolerant sorghum variety next season. First, plant the sorghum on rich, well-drained soil right after you sow the maize. At 3-5 cm stem height, perform the first weeding to keep the field free of weeds. Then apply the striga-tolerant sorghum seed you will use in the following season. After you finish weeding, cut a portion of each sorghum stem that is striga-tolerant and plant it together with your maize. Keep the new sorghum seedlings between 10 and 20 cm tall and do not let them grow too low, which encourages them to become short. If you need help choosing a striga-tolerant sorghum variety, go to ICAT.

The weed is anthelinium, which grows in heavy rain and from mid-June to early July. Pull it out as you go so it does not return. After you have cleared it, weed the sorghum two or three times while the plants are still small. When the sorghum matures, apply 200 kg per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 at a panicle initiation rate of 3 to 5 cm, then a top-dress urea at 100 kg per hectare, and a third application at 50 kg per hectare, using the base fertilizer's fertilizer content as a guide. Make sure the soil is even and the rows are not too close together. For any variety advice, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted weeds so the seed does not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea, which weakens Striga and strengthens your sorghum. history.content: how stop Striga seed buildup

draws.answer: Remove the weeds at harvest so the Cercospora species do not stay in the field. Then, at panicle initiation, top-dress with urea in a 100 kg per hectare split, which is the 50 kg per hectare recommended for the soil, not twice the recommended amount. If a large part of your field shows striga, you should plant a striga tolerant maize variety together with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut; cut the stems at ground level to keep the nodules in the soil. For confirmation of striga and the exact dose, see ICAT.

Use a cereal-lushiage rotation after the legume harvest. Sow a striga tolerant variety together with or in rotation with the legume and cut the legume stems at ground level so the nodules stay in the soil. Do not grow the legume on the same plot for more than two consecutive years, which would let the parasite carry over. Choose a legume that grows well in your region and obtains it from an ICAT for the best variety.

history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink-flowered weed at the base, how can I manage it?

draws.answer: You are dealing with striga in your sorghum crop. Plant a striga-tolerant sorghum variety in the next season, following the usual planting schedule. Then, after the harvest, take a portion of each stalk and cut it at ground level, leaving the nitrogen-fixing root nodules in the soil. After cutting, sow a cereal after the legume to benefit from the nitrogen. If you have any doubts about the variety or need a more resistant variety, consult ICAT.

The problem is from the groundnut rosette virus complex, which causes stunted growth in sorghum and is also visible as leaf yellowing and bunched, distorted young leaves. First, rogue out and destroy the heavily affected sorghum plants to remove the virus source. Then, sow your next sorghum crop early and at the close spacing recommended for dense stands. Keep the field free of weeds to reduce aphid hosts that spread the virus. Choose a tolerant sorghum variety for the next planting. For resistant variety options, contact ICAT.

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No, the two products are not mixed and the product is not thicker. One is an approved product, and the other is a homemade product. The approved one is named on the container: for the control of thrips, pod borers and aphids, an approved product. It contains one active ingredient, which varies by product; the active ingredient list is published for each product. The homemade product is made from groundnut, soya or cowpea powder, and it also contains the agents named on the label, which are not listed here. If your problem changes, the product changes too. Ask ICAT for the current approved product and for its rate before you mix.

No, mixing insecticides does not make a stronger spray, and there is no safe way to mix them. The label you bought from an approved seller says to always use the product at the rate written on it, and it will not tell you the rate of each ingredient. What it says is that the product is approved for the crop and that it is a mix of an approved product and a mineral oil or varnish, and it gives no quantity. The label is written in French on the container, so you should read it and not guess. Ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate before you mix, and if you can, use a approved container.

per_item.reference: You need to vaccinate the healthy goats and sheep with the PPR vaccine after you isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. First, isolate every sheep or goat that has fever, muco-purulent discharge, mouth sores, diarrhoea, coughing or pneumonia. Then seal the herd by stopping any movement of animals in or out. Do not sell or slaughter any animal for market and dispose of any dead animals safely. Give the sick animals clean water and soft feed. After these measures, on veterinary advice give the PPR vaccine to all healthy and in-contact goats and sheep. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My sheep are dying fast from a disease that looks like PPR, what steps save the rest?

draws.answer: There is no treatment and no vaccine for cattle tick-borne disease, so you must act quickly. Call the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine colour; red to black means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade, give it clean water, and do not make it walk. Hand-pick every tick you see on all the sheep, not just the sick one. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will determine the exact disease and prescribe the correct drug and dose. You should see the veterinary service the same day.

It is leucaena poisoning, not a tick-borne disease. First, cut the leucaena back so it is only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never the main feed. Then mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Introduce this new feed mix gradually over several days, and always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the animals keep dying despite these changes, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Support the sick goats and sheep with water and soft feed. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Vaccinate the healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine, but only after veterinary advice. I cannot give you the exact date of the next vaccination campaign, and you should ask the veterinary service for that information.

history.content: When will the next PPR vaccination campaign start in my district

draws.answer: You should vaccinate your chickens against Newcastle disease starting at ~2-3 weeks of age and repeat the vaccination on the schedule recommended by the vaccine provider. First, keep all birds isolated from the sick ones. Then burn or bury any dead chickens and any soiled litter. After that disinfect the chicken house thoroughly. Finally, vaccinate the chickens with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, following the vaccination schedule. If you need help, go to the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.

The next vaccination is recommended for the 6-8 week old, after the first vaccination at 3-6 months. Keep the updated schedule to protect the entire herd from fowl pox. I cannot give you the exact date of the next campaign, but you can ask the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary for that specific timing.

history.content: My sorghum is stunted and I notice a pink-flowered plant wrapping its stems near the ground. How can I manage this?

draws.answer: Pink-flowered plants with stunted growth indicate the plant is infected with a virus. First, rogue out and destroy the most heavily infected plants to cut the source of the virus. Next, plant an improved tolerant sorghum variety in your next season, using an approved fungicide at the labelled rate. Also, do not grow sorghum on the same plot year after year; rotate with a grain legume such as cowpea or soybean. If you need help identifying the disease and getting the correct fungicide, go to ICAT.

The pink-flowered plant is a sign of sorghum rosette, which causes stunted growth. Remove the worst-affected plants from the field right away. After removal, sow the next sorghum seed early and at the close spacing recommended, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts. Choose a tolerant sorghum variety for the following season. You can obtain resistant varieties from ICAT.

per_item.reference: Those symptoms point to PPR, peste des petits ruminants, a fast and highly contagious virus affecting goats. First, isolate every sick goat together and halt all animal movements into or out of the herd. You must not sell or slaughter any goats for market during this outbreak, and any carcasses must be disposed of safely. Provide the sick goats with water and soft feed to support them. After that, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with the PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: All my goats are running a fever, their eyes and noses are full of pus, and a few have died already.

draws.answer: That is a tick-borne disease, and gall sickness is its disease. Call the veterinary service the same day; they alone can tell which disease it is and give the right drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, because red to black points to redwater and yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick goats in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make them walk. Hand-pick every tick you can see on all your cattle, not just the sick ones. Do not use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service is the only one to see for this.

Your goats are likely infected by gall sickness, which is caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness. Keep the affected goats in the shade, provide clean water within reach and do not force them to walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick goats. Do not use the same needle on two animals. You should see the veterinary service the same day.

per_item.reference: Use organic manure together with some urea to weaken Striga and strengthen your sorghum, then earth up the field. history.content: How much urea should I mix with manure to control Striga on my sorghum?

draws.answer: You should mix urea with manure to control Striga on sorghum. First, take a few deep roots of a sorghum plant and cut the nodes at ground level. Place the cutting slanted in a pouch of soil, about 5 cm wide, 15 cm deep and 5 cm high, ensuring the base of the cutting is sealed. Repeat the procedure every 8-10 days and keep the pouch in the shade, using fresh manure every few weeks, and always wear gloves and boots while you work. After the cut, plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field. If you need a demonstration of the pouch method, visit ICAT.

You should first weedy-beneficial soil preparation. When sorghum is young, cut the panicles at ground level and bury the seedlings so the root system stays in the soil. After harvest, apply 150 kg/ha of urea, then later add a 50 kg/ha top-dress fertilizer, and after that use 75 kg/ha of urea. Plant a Mucuna cover in the slow-evolving zone, 2 m by 1 m, about 15,000 plants per hectare. I cannot give you the exact mixture ratio, but ICAT can provide guidance.

Use improved tolerant varieties from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and maintain a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy and never from a mottled or deformed stem. history.content: I found a pink flower weed hugging the bottom of my short sorghum stalks, what steps should I take?

draws.answer: That weed is a sign of striga in your short sorghum. First, pull out and destroy the most badly affected plants to remove the source of the problem. Then, for the next sowing season, plant a striga-tolerant variety, either by mixing the seeds with a cereal or a legume, or by using a specific striga-tolerant variety. After you have the new seed, perform a ground treatment by mixing a strand of ground neem-seed powder 1-2 times into each funnel of the seedlings, which can be repeated every 8-10 days. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant. Finally, go to ICAT to have a striga-tolerant variety confirmed and to obtain the appropriate seed.

The pink flower weed is a symptom of the flower thistles that attack the heads of sorghum, and you must treat it to protect the crop. Apply a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel while the plants are young. One kilogram of this mixture will cover roughly 1,500-2,000 plants, and you must repeat the application every 8-10 days. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After you harvest the sorghum, pull the weeds at ground level and destroy them or bury them, avoiding any spraying. If you later see flower thistles on the field, go to ICAT to obtain a approved product.

per_item.reference: Pull the pink weed by hand before it flowers and burn what you pull up so the seed does not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure and a little urea and earth up to weaken the weed and strengthen the sorghum. history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink weed clinging to its base, how can I fix this?

draws.answer: You say your sorghum is stunted and you see a pink weed sticking to its base. I have to tell you that this crop is not something I was taught, and I will not guess a cause, a product or a dose because that could mislead you. For any crop issue, I recommend you walk the field and look closely at the plants, note which parts are affected, whether the problem is in a single area or across the whole plot, and any recent weather changes. Pull one affected sorghum plant with its roots, keep it in a bag with a few leaves, and do not apply any spray until someone has examined it. Take the sample and your notes to the ICAT extension agent, who can look at the field.

The problem is that sorghum is being attacked by thrips and pod borers, which are sap-sucking insects. Start by opening a shallow drainage channel to let excess water run off the field. Then, apply an approved insecticide at the labelled rate, which you should obtain from ICAT. After the crop is harvested, go through the stored sorghum grain and destroy or deep-bury any infested sorghum grain. When the next season you plant, plant a sorghum variety that is resistant to the insects. For the current approved product and rate, see ICAT.

On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: How do I manage an outbreak of peste des petits ruminants in my flock?

draws.answer: The disease is called "babesiosis". First, keep all cattle well fed and watered to help them fight the infection. Second, separate any sick animals from the healthy ones and do not make them move. Third, dispose of dead animals by burying or burning them, and never sell or eat a sick animal. Fourth, vaccinate the entire herd against babesiosis and the same measure applies to other trypanosomiasis. If the disease is not in your area, you should see the veterinary service.

Peste des petits ruminants is called classical fowl pox. First, isolate the affected animals from the rest of the herd. Provide them with extra feed and clean water while the disease runs its course. Then clear any standing water and tidy the surroundings to cut down mosquito breeding. Vaccinate the whole flock against fowl pox to prevent further cases. For the isolated animals, you should consult the veterinary service.

Pull one affected plant with its roots, keep it in a bag with a few leaves, and do not spray anything until someone has seen it. Take it to the ICAT extension agent, who can look at the field.

After each plant, disinfect your cutting tools before you use them on the next plant. Then, take cuttings only from cassava plants that have no spots, no wilting, and no gum, and plant those cuttings. Plant an improved tolerant cassava variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you later see angular spots with wilting without the other signs, you should go to ICAT for confirmation.

history.content: Can I mix two insecticides in one spray to make it stronger?

Then add the extra chemicals at the same volume, mixing them well so they are even distributed. If the pest pressure is high, ask ICAT for the current approved product and the exact dose. I cannot give you a specific combination or strength, and ICAT is the service to ask for that detail.

No, you must use them separately. First, identify the pest you have by looking at the leaves or the insects. Then follow the label for the correct product, dose and contact time. If the label says to mix, use the approved product at the labelled rate and wear gloves and protect your skin. If not, use only one product at a time, following the label. After you spray, clean the leaf undersides and keep the edges of the plot clear of weeds that host them. For the correct product, consult ICAT.

Tell the vet the colour of the urine you see; red to black means redwater, while yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. history.content: I have cassava brown streak disease in my field. What should I do to stop it spreading?

history.content: How can I control Striga witchweed on my sorghum field?

After the plants reach panicle initiation, apply 2 to 3 kg of the recommended NPK fertilizer per hectare. Then, plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field to cut the Striga. For fields badly attacked by Striga, contact ICAT to obtain tolerant sorghum types and a multi-year rotation strategy.

history.content: There are purple flowers on weeds near my sorghum rows, what should I do right now?

draws.answer: The purple flowers are a sign of striga in your sorghum and you should rogue out and destroy the heavily infested sorghum plants. Then, when the sorghum matures, mix a striga-tolerant sorghum variety with your regular sorghum variety in the rotation. Sow the new striga tolerant sorghum early. For the following season, plant a striga tolerant sorghum variety. You can get striga tolerant sorghum seed at the ICAT for the appropriate variety.

Those purple flowers indicate striga in your sorghum, so you must rogue out and destroy the most severely affected plants to eliminate the source of the problem. After that, sow a striga-tolerant sorghum variety in the next cycle. Remember not to grow sorghum on the same land two years in a row, which helps avoid spreading the infection. Plant the new sorghum at the recommended close spacing to obtain a dense stand. For seed of a striga-tolerant variety, you should contact ICAT.

per_item.reference: The cause is Striga, the witchweed that attaches to sorghum roots. First, pull the Striga weeds by hand before they flower and burn everything you pull up, so the seeds do not spread further. Next, improve the soil by adding organic manure plus a little urea and earth-up the plot, which weakens Striga and strengthens sorghum growth. Then introduce a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in rotation or intercropping to run down the seed bank in the soil. For tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation plan for heavily infested fields, contact ICAT.

history.content: I have sorghum that stays short and yellow, and a purple weed clings to its base, what is the cause?

draws.answer: The short and yellow sorghum is a sign of striga. Pull out and destroy the sorghum plants that are heavily infected. Then, when you plant again, take an improved striga tolerant sorghum variety, and plant it early, following the recommended close spacing. Never use the same field for more than one year, to break the disease cycle. If you need help choosing a tolerant variety, visit ICAT.

The short, uniform sorghum and the purple-flowering weed are typical of striga in your sorghum. Start by pulling up the striga plants and destroying them to remove the source of the disease. After that, plant a striga-tolerant sorghum variety in the next season and cut the striga stems at ground level, keeping only the young leaves in the ground. Avoid using the same ground for sorghum, groundnut or cowpea. You can obtain striga-tolerant seeds from ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not a nutrient deficiency, it is Striga, the parasitic weed that attaches to the roots. You can tell them apart because nutrient deficiency shows no attached weed, while Striga appears as a purple or pink-flowered weed clinging around the base of the stunted plants. Because it is Striga, you must pull the weed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted material to stop seed spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure and some urea and earth up to weaken the parasite. Finally, rotate or intercrop with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to reduce the seed bank. For tolerant varieties and a rotation plan, see ICAT.

history.content: my sorghum looks yellow because of nutrient deficiency, right?

draws.answer: It is not nutrient deficiency; the yellowing you see is a nitrogen shortage on depleted soil. First, read the leaves: yellowing that starts on the old lower leaves and moves up is a sign of nitrogen hunger, not a disease. Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on run-down soil. Third, bring back organic matter by applying manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

The yellowing is caused by a nitrogen shortage in the soil, not by a disease. Open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer away from the stem to prevent burning. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see pale streaks along veins or dead-heart, go to ICAT for diagnosis.

per_item.reference: This is typical of PPR. Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Give the sick animals water and soft feed to help them. On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: That is leucaena poisoning, which is a toxin build-up when leucaena makes up too large a share of the ration. Cut leucaena back to a supplement, keeping it under a quarter of the total feed and never as the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen roughage. Introduce this feed mix gradually over several days, and always provide constant clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the animals keep refusing food, keep the feed mixed, give clean water, and do not let the animals become too thin. If appetite does not recover, or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, see the veterinary service.

This is leucaena poisoning, caused by leucaena feeding too heavily on the crop. Cut the leucaena back so it makes up only a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen plenty of roughage. Change the ration gradually over several days. Always provide constant clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the animals keep refusing to eat, you should contact the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: These observations match PPR, peste des petits ruminants, a fast and highly contagious virus that hits goats hard. You must isolate every sick goat immediately and stop all movement of animals into or out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any goats for market while the disease is present, and make sure any carcasses are disposed of safely. Provide water and soft feed to the sick goats to support them. Then vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with the PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: My goats are dying fast, they have fever, runny eyes and noses, and some have mouth sores, what is the problem?

draws.answer: Fever, runny eyes and noses, and mouth sores together point to a tick-borne disease in your goats: gall sickness. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify whether it is redwater or gall sickness and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red to black signals redwater, yellow-brown without red signals gall sickness. Keep the sick goat in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick every tick you see on all the cattle, not only on the ill goat. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service is the only place to obtain the proper medication.

It is leucaena poisoning caused by leucaena in the feed. Cut the leucaena back so it is only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Mix the reduced leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide enough roughage for the rumen. Change the feed composition gradually over several days while keeping clean water and a mineral or salt source always available. If the animals do not start eating again or you notice continued drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: These symptoms are consistent with PPR. Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Give the sick animals water and soft feed. Vaccinate the healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: My sheep are coughing, have diarrhoea and some are dying fast, what should I do?

draws.answer: It is a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, caused by parasites carried by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. First, hand-pick every tick you can see on all the sheep, not only on the affected animal, because the ticks left on the rest of the herd will infect them next. Then call the veterinary service the same day so they can tell which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, because red urine points to redwater and yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service is the only one you should see for proper treatment.

Those signs are typical of leucaena poisoning. Cut the leucaena back so it makes up only a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide more roughage for the rumen. Introduce any feed change gradually over several days. Ensure the sheep have constant access to clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the cough does not stop or the droppings become black, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: Those are signs of cassava brown streak disease on cassava. First, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy and plant a variety that tolerates the disease. Next, pull out any cassava plants showing the yellow leaf veins or the brown corky rot in the roots and destroy them completely. Also, avoid moving any cuttings from fields where those symptoms appear. Finally, bring a sample to ITRA so they can confirm the presence of cassava brown streak disease, because root symptoms need checking.

history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I dig up the roots they are brown and corky. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs are typical of cassava mosaic disease. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. Next, in the next planting, cut only from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation. Do not take cuttings from any mottled or deformed stem. Use an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help.

Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease, so you must uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants. When you replant, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy, avoiding any mottled or deformed stems. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. No spray will cure the disease. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: Striga, known locally as witchweed, can be managed by first feeding the soil with organic manure and a small amount of urea; this weakens the parasite and boosts sorghum health. Then pull the witchweed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted plants to prevent seed spread. Follow with a rotation or intercrop using a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For severe infestations, see ICAT for tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant Striga, which is the same as the one the brochure refers you to for. First, sow your sorghum on rich, deep, well-drained beds. When the plants reach tillering, about 30 to 35 days after sowing, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each whorl funnel. This treats about 1,500 to 2,000 plants per kilogram of the mixture. Do not apply the neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always pair it with the inert carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old sorghum stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. For a large, affected area, go to ICAT to confirm the problem and receive an approved product.

Striga hermonthica is the weed that appears between the sorghum plants during flowering. First, sow your sorghum at a spacing of 80 cm by 40 cm or 40 cm by 20 cm, using 3- to 5 kg per hectare of treated seed. Weed the field at 15-25 days after sowing and again at about 40 days. Apply the three approved products at the labelled rates: 30 kg per hectare of the first, 15 kg per hectare of the second, and 10 kg per hectare of the third, in each application. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old sorghum stalks and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean. See ICAT for the current approved product and exact dose.
